enrichment.short_title: Roadside breath test upheld despite 20-minute rule argument
key_facts: Steven Grant was convicted of drink-driving and failing to provide a breath specimen after being stopped on the A12 near Chelmsford.
PC Lucas required a breath test at the roadside; Grant claimed he had drunk within the previous five minutes, which the Crown Court found was untrue.
The Crown Court dismissed Grant's appeal and stated a case on whether the breath test requirement was lawful and whether EC/IR approval could be challenged.
Grant argued the officer breached manufacturer instructions by not waiting 20 minutes after the last drink and that the intoximeter should not have been approved.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court to the Administrative Court following dismissal of Grant's appeal against magistrates' convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Both questions answered in favour of the prosecution; appeal dismissed and conviction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a police officer has no reasonable cause to suspect alcohol consumption within the preceding 20 minutes, requiring an immediate breath test under section 6 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 is lawful notwithstanding DPP v Carey; challenges to the Secretary of State's approval of an intoximeter or to device modifications are not matters for individual criminal proceedings, following DPP v Brown, DPP v Texeira and DPP v Memery.
legal_issues: Whether PC Lucas acted bona fide in requiring a breath test without waiting 20 minutes
Application of DPP v Carey to manufacturer instructions on recent alcohol consumption
Whether defendants may challenge EC/IR type approval in individual prosecutions
Whether device modifications can invalidate an approved intoximeter

enrichment.short_title: Section 20 Form 7 valid despite missing landlord details

statutes_considered.title: Assured Tenancies and Agricultural Occupancies (Forms) Regulations 1988

key_facts: Two conjoined appeals concerned possession of assured shorthold tenancies where section 20 Housing Act 1988 notices in Form 7 omitted or misstated the landlord's name and address.
In Osborn v Dior the agent signed Form 7 and gave agent particulars but left the landlord's details blank.
In Marito Holdings v Deneche the landlord's details were completed but incorrectly named a company that was not the true landlord.
The Court of Appeal applied the Ravenseft test of whether notices were substantially to the same effect as the prescribed form.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Conjoined appeals from county court possession orders granting landlords possession on the basis of valid assured shorthold tenancies.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed on the section 20 point by a majority; Osborn appeal dismissed unanimously; Marito appeal dismissed by majority with Sedley LJ dissenting on the misstatement point.
enrichment.ratio: A section 20 notice that omits the landlord's particulars where the agent has signed and given full agent particulars can still be a form substantially to the same effect as Form 7 because the statutory purpose is to inform the tenant that the tenancy is an assured shorthold, not primarily to identify the landlord; objective prejudice to the tenant is irrelevant under the Mannai approach.
legal_issues: Whether Form 7 requires landlord particulars when an agent signs
Application of Ravenseft Properties v Hall and Mannai Investment to section 20 notices
Whether incorrect landlord particulars invalidate a notice
Relevance of special notes for existing tenants on Form 7

enrichment.short_title: Speeding conviction on police estimate upheld on review
key_facts: Mark Graham was convicted in his absence by Worthing magistrates of exceeding a 30 mph speed limit on Broadwater Road, Worthing.
Two experienced traffic officers estimated his speed at not less than 45 mph after he overtook another car on the A12 approach to Langton Road.
Graham appealed to the Crown Court, which dismissed the appeal as hopeless; his father then sought judicial review when a transcript became available.
No mechanical or electronic speed-measuring device was used; prosecution rested on visual estimation by two officers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of the Crown Court's dismissal of an appeal against a magistrates' speeding conviction, following renewed permission on 8 October 2002.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Crown Court conclusion held not Wednesbury unreasonable; claimant ordered to pay £250 costs.
enrichment.ratio: A prosecution for speeding may succeed on the opinion evidence of two witnesses who observed the vehicle, provided section 89(2) of the Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984 is satisfied; on judicial review the High Court will not substitute its own view of the facts where the Crown Court was sure on the evidence and its conclusion was within the range of reasonable decisions.
legal_issues: Whether visual speed estimation by police officers can support a speeding conviction
Application of section 89(2) Road Traffic Regulation Act 1984
Wednesbury unreasonableness of Crown Court factual findings
Scope of judicial review of Crown Court criminal appeals

confidence.notes: Outcome, facts, section 89(2) analysis, and Wednesbury standard are clear. No linked cases are cited in the judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Adjudicator payment enforced despite contract termination

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Levolux subcontracted to Fersons for brise soleil work at Filton; Fersons withheld interim payment and purported to terminate the sub-contract.
An adjudicator found Levolux entitled to £51,659.42 because Fersons' withholding notice did not specify grounds as required by section 111.
Fersons resisted summary enforcement, arguing that post-termination clauses 29.8 and 29.9 extinguished sums due under the adjudicator's decision.
The TCC granted summary judgment enforcing the adjudicator's decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from summary judgment enforcing an adjudicator's decision in ongoing construction contract proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; adjudicator's decision enforceable pending final resolution.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 108 of the Housing Grants Construction and Regeneration Act 1996 an adjudicator's decision is binding and enforceable pending final determination; contractual termination clauses such as clause 29.8 do not override the obligation to pay sums adjudged due where the adjudicator acted within jurisdiction, and Parliament's purpose would be defeated if such clauses prevailed.
legal_issues: Whether contractual termination clauses override adjudicator payment decisions
Enforcement of adjudicator decisions pending arbitration
Interaction of section 108 HGCRA with sub-contract termination provisions
Application of Bouygues v Dahl-Jensen and Nikko Hotels test on jurisdiction

enrichment.short_title: Police discipline allowed after committal discharge
key_facts: Detective Sergeant Redgrave was discharged at committal for conspiring to pervert the course of justice over disclosure of a confidential interview document.
After repeal of section 104 PACE 1984 he was charged with discreditable conduct in police disciplinary proceedings based on substantially the same facts.
The disciplinary board and Moses J held the criminal and disciplinary charges were not the same in substance.
The Attorney-General intervened on whether committal discharge equates to acquittal and whether double jeopardy applies to disciplinary tribunals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review dismissal of challenge to Police Disciplinary Board rulings on delay and double jeopardy/res judicata.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; disciplinary proceedings may continue.
enrichment.ratio: Discharge at committal under section 6 of the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 is not equivalent to acquittal and does not engage double jeopardy; the double jeopardy rule does not apply to disciplinary tribunals even where the criminal standard of proof applies, because disciplinary proceedings serve a different purpose and section 104 PACE was a special statutory protection now repealed without creating a lacuna.
legal_issues: Whether committal discharge is tantamount to acquittal for double jeopardy purposes
Whether double jeopardy or res judicata bars police disciplinary proceedings
Effect of repeal of section 104 PACE 1984
Whether criminal and disciplinary charges are the same in substance

enrichment.short_title: LUL development costs invoice partly recoverable
key_facts: London Underground and Pillar Broadway entered a Development Agreement for retail and leisure works at Fulham Broadway station.
LUL invoiced Pillar £510,247.85 under clause 19 for project costs; Pillar disputed many line items and adequacy of supporting documentation.
Pillar argued clause 19.3 required a compliant invoice with full breakdown as a condition precedent to any payment.
The court found several invoice items unproved as properly incurred but awarded LUL a further £244,776.55.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of LUL's claim for unpaid development costs under clause 19 of the Fulham Broadway Development Agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Judgment for LUL in the sum of £244,776.55; partial recovery only where costs were proved properly incurred.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 19 of the Development Agreement Pillar's obligation is to pay sums properly incurred under clause 19.1, not whatever aggregate figure appears on an invoice; clause 19.3 governs invoicing frequency and requires a breakdown sufficient to show how the total is calculated but is not a condition precedent requiring documentary proof of every cost or perfection of every line item before any sum becomes payable.
legal_issues: Construction of clauses 19.1 and 19.3 of the Development Agreement
Whether invoice defects bar recovery of properly incurred costs
What breakdown satisfies clause 19.3
Burden of proving costs were properly incurred

enrichment.short_title: Prison officer unfair dismissal and failure to redeploy
key_facts: Jacqueline Beart, a prison administrative officer at Swaleside, went on long-term sick leave after a dispute with her line manager over part-time working.
Dr Harvey recommended relocation or redeployment but HM Prison Service never acted on that recommendation.
Private investigators observed Beart at her clothes shop; she was dismissed for outside work while on sick pay after a flawed disciplinary process.
The employment tribunal found unfair dismissal and failure to make a reasonable adjustment; the EAT dismissed the employer's appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal upholding tribunal findings of disability discrimination and unfair dismissal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal findings on reasonable adjustment and unfair dismissal upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to relocate an disabled employee as recommended by occupational health can amount to unlawful discrimination under section 5(2) of the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 where section 6 required assignment to a different place of work and the employer led no evidence that redeployment was unreasonable or justified; a disciplinary investigation may be so inadequate that dismissal falls outside the range of reasonable responses.

Application of Morse v Wiltshire County Council sequential test
Whether failure to comply with section 6 duty was justified

enrichment.short_title: Three-month notice must expire on anniversary date
key_facts: Allscan supplied sanitary waste services to Dougland at Bristol Airport under an informal August 1999 contract terminable on three months' notice at any time.
In January 2000 Allscan sent a standard healthcare quotation with a termination clause requiring at least three months' notice prior to the anniversary date.
Dougland performed and paid under the revised quotation but gave only one month's notice terminating on 9 April 2001.
The district judge held three months' notice at any time applied; the circuit judge held the anniversary-date clause in the quotation was accepted by conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court decision allowing Allscan's appeal and holding wrongful termination for insufficient notice.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; contract terminable only on at least three months' notice expiring on the anniversary date of 19 January.
enrichment.ratio: Where a party sends a standard-form quotation setting out all contractual terms including a new termination clause and the other party performs the contract on those terms, the quotation is accepted by conduct objectively judged; subsequent correspondence about three months' notice cannot be used to construe the original contract contrary to Whitworth Street Estates v Miller.
legal_issues: Whether Allscan's January 2000 quotation varied only price and scope or the entire contract
Acceptance of contractual terms by conduct
Admissibility of post-contract correspondence to construe contract formation
Distinction between three months' notice at any time and notice prior to anniversary date
linked_authorities: Whitworth Street Estates (Manchester) Ltd v Miller
Tanfern Ltd v Cameron-MacDonald

confidence.notes: Contract formation, termination clause construction, and appellate reasoning on district judge error are clearly explained.

enrichment.short_title: Charterer liable for demurrage after tank rejection delay
key_facts: The Nikmary was chartered on Asbatankvoy terms to load gasoil at Sikka; her tanks were rejected as unclean on arrival and passed fit only on 5 December 2000.
Laytime expired on 9 December but the vessel did not berth to load until 2 January 2001 because Reliance had no export cargo commitment for her.
Vitol argued clauses 6, 7 and 30(c) excluded waiting time; owners claimed US$291,691.75 demurrage.
The vessel also called at Limassol for additives and discharged slowly at Thessalonika below the required pumping pressure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of owners' demurrage and related claims under an amended Asbatankvoy charter.
enrichment.outcome: Owners awarded demurrage at Sikka of US$291,691.75; reduced demurrage at Thessalonika; Limassol diesel oil claim rejected; partial disbursement recovery.
enrichment.ratio: Delay after a valid notice of readiness was caused by the charterer's failure to have cargo available within laytime, not by congestion or the vessel's prior unclean condition; clause 6 protects against delay getting into berth over which the charterer has no control but does not excuse failure to supply cargo, and clause 30(c)(v) did not apply because no jointly appointed inspector procedure was invoked.
legal_issues: Whether waiting time at anchorage counted as laytime or demurrage
Construction of clauses 6, 7 and 30(c) of the amended Asbatankvoy charter
Cause of delay after tanks passed fit for loading
Pumping clause breach at discharge port

enrichment.short_title: English jurisdiction clause enforced on mis-delivery claim
key_facts: Metro claimed CSAV mis-delivered goods at Iquique, Chile without production of original bills of lading.
CSAV bills of lading contained clause 24 providing for English law and non-exclusive English High Court jurisdiction.
CSAV applied to stay English proceedings in favour of Chilean arbitration, arguing Chilean law issues and parallel proceedings in Chile.
Metro had separately commenced related claims in Chile after missing the English Hague Rules time bar.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to set aside service out of the jurisdiction and for a declaration that the English court should not exercise jurisdiction, or alternatively a stay.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; English proceedings to continue under the non-exclusive jurisdiction clause.
enrichment.ratio: Parties should ordinarily be held to a freely agreed non-exclusive English jurisdiction clause unless strong reasons appear; foreseeable matters of convenience including foreign law at the place of performance, evidential difficulties, and parallel proceedings in Chile do not outweigh the contractual choice of a neutral forum where the claims fall within the clause and no third-party interests are involved.
